shift.desc: Front has already sorted and threaded the overnight arrivals across three departmental inboxes. The machine has ranked them by recency and rule; the assistant re-ranks them by consequence, spotting that a politely worded third follow-up from a client is the most urgent item in a queue where it sits fourteenth.

shift.task: Overnight call log and voicemail review
shift.desc: Aircall has logged, transcribed and attributed the calls that arrived after hours, matching numbers against CRM records. No human touched this. The output is a list of names, times and reasons that will be read in under four minutes.

A courier with an unaddressed package, an interview candidate forty minutes early, and a contractor who needs escorting to the plant room. Three people, three different destinations, one badge printer, and no system involved beyond the sign-in tablet.

Reclaim.ai's conflict detection surfaces six collisions across the leadership diaries and proposes optimal alternatives for all six. Four are accepted as proposed. The remaining two are the reason a human opens the tool at all.

shift.task: The two the algorithm cannot resolve
shift.desc: One proposed slot puts a departing director in the same room as her replacement before the announcement. The other assumes a vice-president takes meetings before ten, which he does not, and which appears in no calendar rule anywhere. Both are resolved by telephone in under fifteen minutes and leave no digital artefact.

Grammarly produces clean first drafts of four routine letters and a departmental notice. Editing is not proofreading here — it is calibration against a house voice that exists in no style guide, and the rewriting of one paragraph that is technically accurate and tonally certain to cause offence.

Zoom hosts the project review; Otter.ai records, transcribes and generates action items unattended. The assistant is not in the meeting. The transcript will be waiting, complete, coherent and in two places wrong.

Two speakers with similar voices have been conflated, which has assigned a delivery commitment to the wrong department head. Correcting it requires having known who was in the room. This task did not exist five years ago and is now among the highest-consequence twenty minutes of the day.

Notion and Guru surface the most-queried internal articles alongside their staleness. Three describe a procurement process retired in the spring, which means enterprise search has been confidently answering current questions with obsolete truth. Pruning them is unglamorous, unmeasured and the reason retrieval works at all.

The caterer for tomorrow's client day has substituted a dietary-restricted order without notice and the audio-visual cart in the main room has developed a fault. Neither is a scheduling problem. Both require authority to spend, permission to improvise and a telephone.

Automated inventory tracking flags four items below threshold and pre-populates the procurement portal. The assistant overrides two of them, knowing that a department is about to double in size and that the reorder quantity the system calculated is based on a headcount that changes on Monday.

blocks.text: At twenty to eight on a Tuesday morning, before the lifts have found their proper rhythm, a woman on the fourth floor of a mid-sized engineering firm is already reading the overnight residue of other people's decisions. There is a shared inbox that filled while she slept. A scheduling assistant has proposed a Thursday slot for a meeting between the chief engineer and a supplier who once, memorably, walked out on him. A transcription tool has attributed a sentence to the wrong person, and the wrong person is the one who will be held to it. The multifunction printer on the third floor has stopped speaking to the network again. None of this appears in her job description, which still uses the word clerical. All of it will be resolved before ten. The machines will have done a great deal of the typing. She will have done all of the deciding.

sections.label: The Score
sections.title: Two million working lives sit in the gap between fifty-eight and thirty

blocks.caption: The administrative workstation at first light: a multi-line console, a shared inbox, a badge printer and a wall of colour-tabbed files. Almost every object here is now half-automated.
blocks.prompt: A wide, low-light documentary photograph of an administrative workstation at first light in a mid-sized corporate office. A multi-line desk telephone console with illuminated line buttons and a coiled headset sits at the left; two monitors show a shared departmental inbox queue and a colour-blocked shared calendar; a visitor sign-in tablet and a badge printer occupy the counter edge; a wire mail trolley half-loaded with franked envelopes is parked beside a large multifunction scanner; behind it, a wall of lateral filing cabinets with colour-coded confidentiality tabs. Muted daylight through vertical blinds, no people in frame, shallow depth of field, restrained colour.

blocks.text: The Replaceable Index for secretaries and administrative assistants — excluding the legal, medical and executive specialisms, which behave differently — is 30.2%. It is a composite, and like all composites it is more useful taken apart than swallowed whole. Two numbers make it. The first is the automation potential score, 58%: the share of the role's actual work that commercially available systems, in production today rather than in a demonstration video, can in principle perform. The second is the human resistance factor, 48%: the share of that theoretical potential which does not convert into practice because of liability, confidentiality, organisational trust, regulatory sign-off, procurement inertia and the simple fact that somebody has to be answerable when the machine is wrong.

The arithmetic is deliberately unglamorous. RPI equals APS multiplied by one minus HRF, expressed as a percentage. Fifty-eight per cent of capability, discounted by forty-eight per cent of friction, yields 30.2%. The gap between the 58 and the 30.2 is the most interesting territory in this entire study, because it is not a rounding error or a measurement artefact. It is the working life of nearly two million people. It is the difference between what a system can do in a controlled pilot and what an organisation will actually permit it to do unsupervised on a Tuesday, with a regulator's deadline approaching and a chief executive's diary in play.

The role decomposes into eighteen distinct task clusters. Three of them remain essentially traditional — performed the way they were performed a decade ago, with better tooling but no meaningful machine substitution. Eleven are augmented: the machine now does a substantial first pass and the human does the second, which is usually the pass that matters. Four did not exist in this role in any recognisable form ten years ago and exist now precisely because the machines arrived. That last group is the story most coverage of clerical automation misses entirely.

The cognitive and physical automation scores diverge sharply. Cognitively, the role scores 58% — routing, drafting, scheduling, summarising, retrieving, proofreading, all of it now within reach of general-purpose language systems and specialised workflow tools. Physically, it scores 8%. The residue is small but stubborn: the mail that arrives on paper because a counterparty's compliance department insists on it, the badge handed across a counter, the audio-visual cart wheeled into a room where the ceiling projector has failed, the catering tray that arrives at the wrong door. Eight per cent is not much. It is also not zero, and it is the anchor that keeps the role tethered to a physical building.

blocks.label: Empirical anchor
blocks.text: In Gallup's Q2 2026 workplace AI survey — fielded 6-20 May 2026 among 22,573 employed U.S. adults, margin of error plus or minus 0.9 points, published 20 July 2026 — 52% of U.S. workers said they use AI in their role, with 30% using it frequently, meaning a few times a week or more. Forty-seven per cent said their organisation had integrated AI tools to improve productivity, efficiency or quality, up six points from 41% the previous quarter, growth Gallup itself described as sharp. Among AI users, the most common applications were writing and editing (51%), search or research (49%) and general assistance or problem-solving (39%). Those three categories are, almost verbatim, the augmented core of the administrative assistant's day.

Forty-two per cent of the role is scored as untouched: work for which no currently deployed system offers a credible substitution path at any price. This is not a residual category of leftovers. It contains the judgement calls that hold an office together — reading a visitor's face and deciding whether the interruption is worth the chief engineer's afternoon, knowing which of two vice-presidents must be seated furthest from the door, understanding that a form's instructions and a regulator's expectations are not the same document.

The AI job creation index sits at 12%. That figure counts new task-load generated by the technology itself and absorbed by this role rather than by a new job title: correcting machine transcription, resolving the scheduling conflicts an algorithm cannot navigate because they are political rather than temporal, curating the knowledge bases that AI search tools depend on, and providing first-line technical support and training to colleagues who have been handed tools nobody taught them to use. Twelve per cent is a modest number that does a great deal of work. It explains why the role's headcount has not collapsed in line with the capability curve.

The overall band is Moderate, on a five-to-ten-year horizon. That is a specific and deliberately unexciting claim. It is not a prediction that the job disappears; it is a prediction that the job's centre of gravity moves, and that the movement is slow enough to be managed and fast enough to be felt. Against a base of 1,944,000 U.S. workers and a median annual wage of $46,290, the Bureau of Labor Statistics projects employment growth of -1.6%. A gentle decline, not a cliff — which is exactly what an index of 30.2% with a resistance factor of 48% should produce.

One caution about what this score is not. It is not a measure of how safe any individual's job is, because automation does not arrive evenly across an economy; it arrives first where procurement is centralised, tooling is standardised and the work is already documented. Nor is it a measure of quality. A system can perform a task at 58% of the standard a competent human sets and still be scored as capable, because organisations frequently accept degraded output in exchange for speed. The index measures displacement pressure. It does not measure whether the displacement is a good idea.

sections.label: The Shift
sections.title: Interrupted all day by software that cannot make the decision

blocks.text: Abstractions about task decomposition dissolve on contact with an actual working day. The day below is a composite, assembled from the eighteen task clusters and the tooling that vendors have actually shipped into production, not from a roadmap. What it shows is not a human being gradually replaced by software. It shows a human being repeatedly interrupted by software that has finished its portion of a job and needs a decision it cannot make.

Notice the rhythm. The automated blocks are early and short — overnight call logs transcribed, a meeting recorded, inventory thresholds crossed. The augmented blocks are long and dense, clustered around late morning and early afternoon, and every one of them is a two-stage operation: machine draft, human judgement. The purely human blocks are the ones with a stranger in them, a regulator behind them, or a room full of people waiting.

blocks.caption: Mid-morning triage. The left monitor holds the shared inbox; the right holds a conflict the scheduling assistant has flagged but cannot resolve.
blocks.prompt: Over-the-shoulder candid photograph of an administrative assistant wearing a slim headset, triaging a shared departmental inbox on the left monitor while an AI scheduling assistant flags a calendar conflict on the right monitor. Sticky notes with extension numbers ring the monitor bezels; a spiral desk diary lies open beside the keyboard; a multi-line phone console at the edge of frame shows three lines illuminated. Warm office lighting, mid-morning, documentary realism, no branding visible.

blocks.text: The single most revealing entry is the early-afternoon transcription review. A meeting has been recorded and summarised automatically; the summary is coherent, well-formatted and confidently wrong about who said the thing that commits a department to a deadline. Correcting it takes twenty minutes and requires knowing the voices in the room. This task did not exist five years ago. It exists now solely because the tool exists, and it is now among the highest-consequence things the role does, because an uncorrected action item propagates into project plans and performance reviews.

The second most revealing entry is the one that never appears on any productivity dashboard: the ten minutes spent deciding not to book a meeting the algorithm proposed. There is no artefact, no output, no ticket closed. The value created is entirely negative — a bad outcome that did not happen. Every measurement system currently sold to enterprises is structurally blind to it, which turns out to matter enormously when the time comes to justify a headcount.

sections.label: The Anatomy
sections.title: Eleven augmented, three intact, four that the machines themselves created

blocks.text: Eighteen task clusters, sorted three ways. The sorting is the analysis. A role is not automated or not automated; it is a bundle of jobs with wildly different exposure, and the bundle can lose two-thirds of its content while retaining all of its headcount, or shed half its headcount while retaining all of its content. Which of those happens depends on how the remaining tasks distribute across people.
The augmented eleven

The largest block by far. Call handling is now mediated by caller identification and CRM integration, so the routing decision arrives pre-loaded with context — but the decision itself, which caller is genuinely urgent and which merely insistent, remains human. Database and spreadsheet maintenance runs on templates and validation rules that catch the malformed entry but not the plausible one entered against the wrong project. Email workflow coordination is the archetype: shared inboxes with response prioritisation, in which the machine sorts and the human decides what sorting means when a client's third follow-up is politely worded and quietly furious.

Drafting is where augmentation is most visible and least understood. AI writing assistants produce a serviceable first draft of routine correspondence in seconds. What follows is not editing in the copy-desk sense; it is calibration against an organisational voice that exists nowhere in written form. A letter that is technically correct and tonally wrong does more damage than one that is late. The same pattern governs proofreading, which has quietly inverted: the role now spends more time checking documents produced by staff using AI tools than documents typed by hand, and the error profile has changed from typographic to substantive.

Filing has become genuinely hybrid, and the hybridity is the difficulty. Cloud document management handles the structured case; paper persists wherever a counterparty, an auditor or a jurisdiction demands it. The retrieval task — finding a document from a partial or ambiguous description, which is how humans actually ask for things — is the part search tools handle worst, because the query is not a query. It is a memory: the one with the blue letterhead, from around the time of the merger.

blocks.caption: The hybrid record. Cloud document management on the screen, hanging folders tabbed by project, date and confidentiality on the wall, and a sheet-fed scanner arbitrating between them.
blocks.prompt: A hybrid records environment photographed plainly: a bank of open lateral filing drawers with hanging folders tabbed in three distinct colours for project, date and confidentiality level, directly beside a high-speed sheet-fed document scanner mid-job with a stacked output tray, and a laptop displaying a cloud document management folder tree. A cross-cut shredder bin and a carton of archival folders sit on the floor. Fluorescent overhead lighting, unglamorous, precise, no people.

blocks.text: The traditional three

Greeting visitors survives intact, and not for sentimental reasons. The task requires assessing a stranger's purpose and urgency in real time, translating an ambiguous request into the correct internal destination, and managing physical flow when three parties arrive at once. Every component is a judgement made under time pressure with incomplete information and a live human being watching. Kiosks handle the subset where the visitor already knows who they are meeting — which is precisely the subset that never needed a receptionist.

Form completion resists for a different reason: liability. Interpreting instructions, gathering inputs from several systems and ensuring compliance with both internal policy and external regulation is work in which being confidently wrong is worse than being slow. Language models are optimised for fluency, and fluency is exactly the wrong failure mode when a regulator reads the output. Event logistics resists for a third reason again — venue, catering, audio-visual and attendee communications are a real-time contingency problem in which the plan's value collapses the moment a supplier fails, and recovery requires authority to spend, permission to improvise and a telephone.
The created four

These are the twelve per cent made visible. First-line technical support for office software, printers and scanners, plus training colleagues on organisational systems — a burden that migrated to this role because it sits closest to everyone. Managing AI scheduling outputs by resolving what the algorithm structurally cannot: unwritten hierarchy, personal preference, politically sensitive combinations of people in one room. Reviewing machine-generated transcriptions and action items, correcting speaker attribution and disambiguating statements. And curating the organisational knowledge base and intranet so that AI search returns accurate results as workflows change.

That last one deserves emphasis. Enterprise AI search is only as good as the corpus beneath it, and corpora rot. Somebody has to notice that a process document describes a system decommissioned in the spring, and that the retrieval tool is now confidently answering questions with obsolete truth. The person who notices is, overwhelmingly, the administrative assistant — because they are the only person who touches every department's documents and has an incentive to keep them findable.

sections.label: The Innovators
sections.title: Ten vendors, twenty couplings, and not one that greets a stranger

blocks.text: Ten vendors carry documented evidence against this role's task set, and the shape of their coverage is more informative than any individual product claim. They cluster, and the clusters map almost exactly onto the augmented eleven — not onto the traditional three, and only partially onto the created four. Nobody is selling a product that greets a visitor.

Notion is the broadest, touching six of the role's tasks at an average automation potential of 54% — the lowest average in the set, which is what breadth costs. It is a late-stage private company shipping in production, and its published customer evidence is instructive: Notion's AI features, powered by Claude, are described as helping large enterprises reduce time spent searching for information, with Osaka Gas estimating a 35% reduction, and Notion AI saving customers such as Remote an estimated ten minutes per search across three hundred daily queries. Those are search-and-retrieval claims. They map onto the research, filing and knowledge-curation clusters, and they say nothing at all about scheduling judgement or visitor management.

At the opposite end sits Otter.ai, covering a single task at 80% — the highest automation potential recorded here. Transcription is the cleanest automation case in the entire role: bounded input, bounded output, objectively checkable, and a task humans have always found tedious. It is also the task that generated a new human job, transcript correction, almost immediately. Eighty per cent capability plus twenty per cent consequential error is not a labour-saving equation; it is a labour-transforming one.

Reclaim.ai is the second-highest at 73% across two tasks, and it is the youngest company in the set — seed or early growth stage, with roughly six million dollars or more raised including a $4.8m seed round. It sells calendar automation with conflict detection, which is precisely the capability that produced one of this role's four created tasks: managing the outputs the algorithm cannot resolve. Front, at Series D with more than two hundred million dollars raised and a unicorn valuation, covers shared inbox and correspondence routing at 70%. Zoom, public and in production, matches it at 70% on meeting workflow.

blocks.caption: The exception queue. Two flagged conflicts the scheduling assistant surfaced, an annotated org chart under the keyboard, and a phone off its cradle.
blocks.prompt: Close crop of a desk monitor displaying an AI scheduling assistant's proposed meeting slots with two conflicts visibly flagged in amber, a small handwritten note taped to the monitor bezel, a desk telephone handset lying off its cradle in the foreground, and a printed organisational chart annotated in pencil lying half under the keyboard. Shallow focus resting on the annotated chart. Quiet, procedural, cool office light, no legible branding.

blocks.text: Grammarly, profitable and late-stage private with substantial recurring revenue, covers drafting and proofreading at 68%. Guru, venture-backed across multiple rounds, and Atlassian, public and in production, both sit at 65% on knowledge management — the infrastructure layer beneath the curation task. Five9 is the outlier on deployment status: a public, established contact-centre-as-a-service vendor scoring 75% on call handling, but recorded here at pilot rather than production for this role. Aircall, growth-stage and venture-backed, covers cloud telephony at 55% in production.

Three patterns are worth naming. First, the highest scores go to the narrowest products. Otter at 80% does one thing; Notion at 54% does six. This is the inverse of how enterprise software is usually sold, and it corresponds directly to the warning issued by one of the category's own founders, quoted later in this piece. Second, the funding profile skews mature — a public company, a unicorn, a profitable late-stage private, several venture-backed growth companies. This is not a speculative market waiting for capability; it is a market with revenue, which means the deployment curve is a procurement question, not a research question.

Third, and most consequential, the coverage map has a hole in exactly the shape of the human fortress. Ten vendors, twenty task-couplings, and none of them addresses reception judgement, regulatory form completion or day-of event recovery. That is not because those tasks are trivial. It is because they are unbounded, physically situated and legally consequential — three properties that make a product hard to sell and a demonstration impossible to stage. The market is efficient. It has gone where the bounded problems are, and it has left the ambiguous ones on the desk.

sections.label: The Cautionary Tales
sections.title: Forty-five redundancies, rescinded in a month by rising call volumes

blocks.text: The most instructive failure in clerical automation to date was not a technical failure. The system worked. The measurement did not, and the measurement is what people were made redundant on.

In July 2025, Commonwealth Bank of Australia announced that forty-five customer-service roles in its Customer Service Direct business were redundant following the deployment of an AI-powered voice bot, which the bank said had cut call volumes by two thousand a week. The logic was clean and the arithmetic looked sound: fewer calls arriving, therefore fewer people needed to answer them. Within weeks the announcement had come apart. Following pressure from the Finance Sector Union, and evidence that call volumes were in fact rising — the bank was offering overtime and drafting team leaders onto the phones — CBA reversed the decision. It admitted that its initial assessment had not adequately considered all relevant business considerations and that the roles were not redundant. The reversal was reported on 21 and 22 August 2025.

Two details of the reversal repay attention. The first is mechanical: the affected staff were not rehired after termination. Their redundancy declarations were rescinded, and they were offered a choice — remain in their roles, seek redeployment within the bank, or proceed with the redundancy package. That distinction matters because it reveals how fast the decision had moved and how early the intervention landed. The second is linguistic. The phrase about relevant business considerations is a masterpiece of institutional deflection, and it conceals a specific and common error: the bank measured deflection at the front door and inferred workload behind it.

That inference is wrong in a particular and generalisable way. A voice bot removes the simplest calls first, because simple calls are what it can handle. What remains is a residue of harder, longer, more emotionally charged interactions — the ones that were escalated, the ones where the bot failed and the customer is now calling for the second time and is furious about it. Call volume falls. Handling time per call rises. Total human labour may not fall at all, and can rise. Every dashboard in the deployment will show green.

Apply that mechanism to the administrative assistant's day and it recurs everywhere. Automated call routing deflects the caller who knows which extension they want; what reaches the desk is the caller who does not know, cannot explain, and has already been transferred twice. Template libraries handle routine inquiries; what reaches the human is the inquiry that resembles a template but is not one, which is the most dangerous category because it invites a template answer. AI conflict detection resolves the scheduling collisions that are merely temporal; what arrives on the desk is the collision that is political, and those take longer than any of the ones the machine absorbed.

The second cautionary pattern is subtler and has no headline attached to it: the correction tax. Machine output that is 80% correct does not save 80% of the labour, because the human must read 100% of it to find the 20% that is wrong. Transcription is the canonical case — speaker misattribution in a meeting record is invisible to anyone who was not in the room, propagates silently into project plans and performance conversations, and is discovered weeks later when somebody is held to a commitment they did not make. Verification is not a diminished form of production. It is a different and in some respects harder skill, and it is currently being asked of people whose job titles have not changed and whose grades have not moved.

The third pattern is corpus decay. Enterprise AI search is sold on the promise that institutional knowledge becomes instantly retrievable, and the evidence from vendors supports the retrieval claim — Osaka Gas's estimated 35% reduction in time spent searching is a real and substantial gain. But retrieval quality is downstream of curation quality, and curation is invisible, unrewarded maintenance work. A knowledge base that nobody prunes does not degrade gracefully into unhelpfulness; it degrades into confident wrongness, answering current questions with decommissioned truth. The organisations that capture the search gain are the ones that quietly funded a curator. The ones that treated the tool as self-sustaining bought themselves an authoritative-sounding archive of obsolete process.

The common thread across all three is that the failure never appears where the automation was installed. It appears one step downstream, in the residue, in the verification, in the maintenance — and downstream is precisely where the administrative assistant sits. This is why a role with 58% automation potential produces an index of 30.2% rather than something close to 58%. The resistance factor of 48% is not superstition or Luddism. It is, substantially, the accumulated institutional memory of deployments that looked like CBA's in July and looked rather different by August.

sections.label: Around the World
sections.title: Japan legislates the transition; America's resistance is revocable by memorandum

blocks.text: The American figure of 30.2% is a national artefact, shaped by American procurement habits, American employment law and an American tolerance for reorganisation. Move the same task bundle across borders and the automation potential barely shifts — the tasks are the tasks — while the resistance factor moves considerably. Two jurisdictions illustrate the range, and both complicate the story rather than confirming it.

Japan approved its AI Promotion Act on 28 May 2025. Coverage of the law's labour-market implications flags administrative clerks and routine public-sector processing — permit handling, hotline responses, basic audits — as the functions most exposed to near-term AI automation, while pushing remaining staff towards supervisory and judgement-based work. That last clause is the entire thesis of this piece restated as national policy. It is not a displacement narrative; it is a reallocation narrative, and it is being written into statute rather than discovered after the fact by a bank's human resources department.

blocks.caption: Routine public-sector processing: the permit counter, where policy documents in Tokyo and vendor roadmaps in San Francisco point at the same desk.
blocks.prompt: A municipal administrative service counter in Japan, photographed straight on and plainly: a numbered ticket display above the counter, tiered plexiglass trays holding stacks of pre-printed application forms, a clerk seated at a terminal beside an automated document-issuing kiosk, a stamp pad and tray at the counter edge, a queue rope and a row of waiting chairs in soft focus behind. Even daylight through large windows, calm, orderly, documentary tone, no legible text or signage.

blocks.text: It is worth being careful about the evidentiary weight here. The clearest statement of which Japanese functions are exposed comes from trade coverage, not from a statistical agency, and trade coverage of automation has a well-documented directional bias. The OECD's report on AI use in the Japanese workplace exists precisely as a regulator-grade counterweight — an examination of how artificial intelligence is actually diffusing through Japan's labour market, useful for grounding adoption-rate claims rather than accepting vendor-adjacent narratives about clerical automation at face value. Any serious reading of Japan's trajectory should anchor on the former and treat the latter as a hypothesis about direction, not a measurement of magnitude.

Structurally, Japan compresses the resistance factor from both ends. Its administrative culture is unusually document-dense and process-formal, which raises automation potential — formalised process is machine-readable process. But the same culture places extraordinary weight on the correctness and provenance of documents, and on the human accountable for them, which raises resistance. The Act's framing, pushing staff towards supervisory work, is an attempt to resolve that tension by redefining the job rather than eliminating it. Whether that redefinition arrives with commensurate grading and pay is the question the statute does not answer.

Latin America and the Caribbean present the opposite configuration. The World Bank estimates that 30-40% of jobs in the region are exposed in some way to generative AI, with generative AI putting 2-5% of jobs at risk of automation outright. The gap between those two ranges is the whole argument of this piece rendered at continental scale: exposure is not displacement, and the ratio between them is roughly an order of magnitude. Exposed jobs in the region are more likely to be urban, formal and higher-paying, and to require higher education — which inverts the folk assumption that automation arrives first for the least advantaged.

Two honest caveats attach to that estimate. The World Bank's own publication page for the same research gives the exposure range as 26-38% rather than 30-40%, a discrepancy small enough to be a methodological revision and large enough to be worth naming rather than smoothing over. And the brief does not identify specific occupations at all. The occupational inference comes from the related ILO-World Bank working paper, which associates automation risk in the region with the banking, finance, insurance and public-administration sectors — four sectors that between them employ a very large share of the region's administrative and clerical workforce. The inference is reasonable. It is still an inference.

What emerges from the comparison is a pattern rather than a ranking. Wherever administrative work is formal, documented and concentrated in large institutions — Japanese public administration, Latin American banking, American corporate services — automation potential is high and rises with formality. Wherever accountability is personal, legally consequential and physically situated, resistance is high and rises with consequence. The index for this role in the United States, 30.2%, sits close to the low end of the World Bank's regional exposure range and far above its outright-automation range, which is roughly where a bundle of eleven augmented tasks, three traditional ones and four newly created ones ought to sit.

The divergence to watch over the next five years is not capability, which will be broadly uniform across these markets because the vendors are global and the models are the same. It is the institutional response. Japan is legislating a supervisory transition. Australia's largest bank, as the previous section recounted, attempted a redundancy transition and reversed it inside a month under union pressure. The United States has neither statute nor, in most of this workforce, union coverage — which means its resistance factor of 48% is composed almost entirely of managerial caution, liability fear and procurement inertia. Those are real forces. They are also, unlike legislation and collective agreements, revocable by a single memorandum.

sections.label: The Human Fortress
sections.title: Presence, consequence and an organisational map that exists in no corpus

blocks.text: Forty-two per cent of this role is scored untouched — not partially automated, not augmented, but outside the reach of any deployed system at any price. In a study of automation, that is the number most likely to be misread as nostalgia. It is not. It is a structural finding, and the structure has three walls.

The first wall is embodied presence. Physical automation potential for this role is 8%, and the tasks in that residue are not incidental. Someone must be at the counter when a courier arrives with a package requiring a signature and no scheduled recipient. Someone must be in the room when the projector fails eleven minutes before a board presentation. Someone must physically hand a badge to a stranger and, in the act of handing it, decide whether this person should be walked to the meeting room or left to find it. Presence is not a task that automation performs badly. It is a task automation does not perform.

blocks.caption: The task no vendor sells: an unscheduled visitor, a waiting appointment, and a third line ringing, all resolved in about eleven seconds.
blocks.prompt: Candid documentary photograph at an office reception counter mid-morning. An administrative assistant stands to greet an unscheduled visitor holding a delivery clipboard, while a second visitor waits on a bench nearby with a laptop bag, and a multi-line telephone console behind the counter shows a line illuminated. Visitor badges fanned on the counter beside a sign-in tablet and a bowl of spare lanyards. Natural window light, the assistant caught mid-gesture directing traffic, warm and unposed, no legible signage.

blocks.text: The second wall is consequence asymmetry. Consider form completion — interpreting instructions, assembling inputs from several sources, ensuring compliance with internal policy and external regulation. Every individual step is mechanisable. The bundle is not, because the cost function is violently asymmetric: a form completed slowly costs a day, a form completed wrongly costs a licence, a fine or a lawsuit. Language systems are optimised to produce fluent, plausible output, and plausibility under regulatory scrutiny is precisely the wrong virtue. An assistant who is unsure stops and asks. A model that is unsure produces a confident sentence, because that is what it was trained to do.

The third wall is the organisational map — the single most underrated asset in this occupation and the one least legible to software. An experienced assistant holds an unwritten model of an institution: who actually approves things as opposed to who signs them, which two departments are in a quiet dispute, which executive will not take a meeting before ten, whose deputy must be copied or offence will be taken. None of this is in the directory. Almost none of it is in any document at all, which means it is absent from every corpus any retrieval tool indexes. It is acquired by being present for years and paying attention.

This is why one of the four newly created tasks is what it is: managing AI scheduling outputs by resolving conflicts the algorithm cannot navigate — unwritten hierarchy rules, personal preferences, politically sensitive meeting combinations. The tool did not eliminate the need for the map. It made the map more valuable, by removing the mechanical work that used to surround it and leaving the judgement exposed. A scheduling assistant that proposes an optimal slot has solved a calendar problem. Whether that slot puts two people in a room who should not currently be in a room together is not a calendar problem, and no amount of additional calendar data will make it one.

The human resistance factor of 48% is largely these three walls expressed as institutional behaviour. Confidentiality classification is a resistance factor: the hybrid filing task explicitly organises documents by confidentiality level, and organisations are conspicuously reluctant to route their most sensitive material through third-party systems regardless of the vendor's assurances. Accountability is a resistance factor: somebody must be nameable when a regulator asks who completed the form. Trust is a resistance factor, and it is not irrational — it is the accumulated memory of tools that were confidently wrong.

There is a further consideration that the index cannot capture. Gallup's Q2 2026 data records that among AI users the most common applications are writing and editing, search or research, and general assistance or problem-solving — three categories that describe the assistive half of this job almost exactly. What it also records is that 52% of U.S. workers use AI in their role and 30% use it frequently, meaning the majority of use is occasional. Occasional use is not the profile of a technology that has absorbed a job. It is the profile of a tool people reach for on particular tasks and set down again, which is what the augmented eleven look like from the inside.

The fortress, then, is not a place where the technology stopped. It is the part of the work that was always the work, obscured for a century by the typing. Strip out the transcription, the routing, the retyping and the first-draft prose, and what remains is a role that is denser in judgement than it has ever been. That is not consolation. It is a warning about grading, because a job that is 42% pure judgement and pays a median of $46,290 has a pricing problem that automation did not create but has made considerably more visible.

sections.label: Industry Voices
sections.title: Vendors sell capability, surveys measure adoption, nobody publishes displacement

blocks.text: There are three constituencies talking about this role, and they are not talking to each other. The vendors describe capability. The workers, through survey instruments, describe usage. The institutions — unions, regulators, banks reversing decisions — describe consequence. Each has a partial and internally consistent view, and the gaps between them are where the interesting claims live.

Start with the vendor constituency, and specifically with an unusually candid statement from inside it. David Shim, co-founder and chief executive of Read AI, told GeekWire in October 2025 something that cuts directly against his own category's marketing.
The approach of agents doing everything is not the right approach. If you try to do everything, you're not going to do anything well.
blocks.cite: David Shim, Co-founder and CEO, Read AI, speaking to GeekWire, 23 October 2025

blocks.text: Read that against this study's vendor evidence and it stops being a platitude and becomes a prediction that the data confirms. The highest automation potential recorded here belongs to Otter.ai at 80%, covering exactly one task. The lowest belongs to Notion at 54%, covering six. The breadth-versus-depth trade-off is visible in the numbers, and it holds across the set: Reclaim.ai at 73% over two tasks, Front at 70% over two, Grammarly at 68% over two, Guru at 65% over two. The narrow tools perform; the broad platforms integrate. Both are useful. Only one of them is the thing being sold when a vendor promises an autonomous assistant.

Shim's point has a second edge that matters more for this occupation. If no single agent should attempt everything, then a role composed of eighteen heterogeneous tasks cannot be addressed by an agent at all — it must be addressed by a portfolio of tools, and a portfolio of tools requires an integrator. The integrator is a person. This is the mechanism by which the technology that was supposed to eliminate the coordinating role instead increases demand for coordination, and it is why the automation potential of 58% translates to an index of 30.2% rather than to a mass redundancy.

The worker constituency speaks through Gallup, and speaks more cautiously than either vendors or commentators. In the Q2 2026 survey — 22,573 employed U.S. adults, fielded over two weeks in May, margin of error under one point — 52% reported using AI in their role, and 30% reported using it frequently. Forty-seven per cent said their organisation had integrated AI tools to improve productivity, efficiency or quality, up six points from 41% the previous quarter. Gallup characterised that quarterly movement as sharp growth, and on a single-quarter basis it plainly is.

But note what the same instrument does not say. It measures adoption, not substitution. A worker reporting frequent AI use is reporting that a tool has entered their workflow, not that a portion of their job has left it. The three leading uses — writing and editing at 51%, search or research at 49%, general assistance or problem-solving at 39% — are all first-pass activities whose output requires a second pass. This is the statistical signature of augmentation, and it is routinely presented in coverage as the statistical signature of replacement. The distinction is not academic. It is the difference between a workforce being retooled and a workforce being retired.

The institutional constituency speaks loudest when something goes wrong, and its most articulate recent statement was made by Commonwealth Bank of Australia, under duress, in August 2025: that its initial assessment did not adequately consider all relevant business considerations. Behind that sentence stands the Finance Sector Union, which supplied the pressure, and a set of operational facts — rising call volumes, overtime offers, team leaders drafted onto phones — that contradicted the bank's own automation dashboard. In the absence of the union, it is not obvious that the contradiction would have surfaced before the terminations completed.

That is the structural asymmetry worth naming as this section closes. Vendors publish capability claims and customer case studies, and the good ones, like the Notion evidence cited earlier, are specific and checkable — Osaka Gas's estimated 35% reduction in search time, Remote's estimated ten minutes saved per search across three hundred daily queries. Survey houses publish adoption rates. Neither publishes displacement data, because neither has it. The only organisations that know whether an automation deployment reduced headcount are the employers, and they disclose it selectively, usually at the moment of announcement and rarely at the moment of reversal. For an occupation of 1,944,000 people, that is a thin evidentiary base on which to be making decisions.

sections.label: The Economics
sections.title: A job partly protected by how little it already pays

blocks.text: The economics of this occupation are peculiar, and the peculiarity is the point: a role with 58% automation potential, sitting in the crosshairs of ten funded vendors, is projected by the Bureau of Labor Statistics to decline by just 1.6%. Not to collapse. To drift. Understanding why requires taking the money apart the way we took the index apart.

Start with the base. 1,944,000 U.S. workers at a median annual wage of $46,290. That wage is the single most important variable in the deployment calculus, and it cuts both ways. It is high enough that a tool which genuinely removes a substantial share of the work has a plausible payback period, which is why the vendor field is crowded. It is low enough that the savings from removing part of one person's work are modest in absolute terms — and modest absolute savings do not survive contact with implementation cost, integration cost, training cost and the risk premium an organisation attaches to being wrong in front of a regulator.

This is the arithmetic that the human resistance factor of 48% encodes. Resistance is usually described in cultural terms — people do not like change — but in this occupation it is overwhelmingly economic and legal. Routing the confidentiality-classified filing system through a third-party platform requires a data protection review. Letting a model complete a compliance form requires someone to own the output. Each of those requirements has a cost, and each cost is subtracted from a saving that was never enormous to begin with. At a median wage twice as high, the same 58% capability would convert into a substantially higher index. The job is partially protected by being underpaid, which is not a comfortable finding.

Now the credit side. The AI job creation index of 12% represents work that flows towards this role rather than away from it, and its economics are the opposite of the displacement story. Correcting machine transcription, resolving algorithmically intractable scheduling conflicts, curating the corpus behind enterprise search, and supporting and training colleagues on tools nobody explained — these are, task for task, harder than the work they displaced. They require judgement, institutional knowledge and the ability to detect confident error. In a functioning labour market that combination reprices upward.

There is little evidence that it has. The projected decline of 1.6% describes headcount, not composition, and composition is where the change is concentrated. The role is losing its low-skill content — retyping, manual sorting, first-draft prose, manual transcription — while retaining all of its high-skill content and acquiring new high-skill content. That is skill compression: the same title, the same grade, the same median, and a materially harder job. It is a well-documented pattern in occupations undergoing augmentation rather than substitution, and it tends to show up in retention statistics long before it shows up in wage statistics.

The productivity evidence, meanwhile, is real but narrower than it is usually presented. Osaka Gas's estimated 35% reduction in time spent searching for information is a substantial operational gain. Remote's estimated ten minutes saved per search across three hundred daily queries is a large aggregate number. Both are search-and-retrieval measurements. Neither is a headcount measurement, and the step from one to the other is exactly where Commonwealth Bank came unstuck: time saved on a task is not the same as a person made redundant, because saved time redistributes into the residue of harder work that the automation left behind.

For employers, the honest conclusion is that this occupation is a poor candidate for headcount reduction and an excellent candidate for scope expansion. The organisations extracting genuine value are not the ones running fewer assistants; they are the ones whose assistants now cover more departments, own the knowledge base, run first-line tool support and act as the human exception-handler for four or five automated workflows. That is a productivity gain of a real kind. It is also a redefinition of the job that most job descriptions, most grading structures and most performance frameworks have not caught up with.

For workers, the arithmetic points somewhere specific. The tasks with the highest automation potential in this role are the ones with the cleanest boundaries — transcription at 80%, calendar automation at 73%, call handling at 75% in pilot. The tasks with no vendor coverage at all are the ones that are physically situated, legally consequential or politically delicate. Anyone in this occupation deciding where to invest their next five years has been handed an unusually legible map: move towards the ambiguity, because the ambiguity is where the money will eventually have to go, and towards the four created tasks, because those are net new demand generated by the technology rather than a rearguard defence against it.

sections.label: Looking Ahead
sections.title: Spread thinner, regraded or unbundled — procurement decides, not capability

blocks.text: The band is Moderate and the horizon is five to ten years. That is a claim about pace, and pace in this occupation is governed by procurement cycles and liability appetite rather than by model capability, which is why it can be stated with more confidence than most forecasts in this field. The capability required to automate the augmented eleven substantially already exists and is in production at ten funded vendors. Almost everything that happens next is an institutional question.
Three trajectories are plausible, and they are not mutually exclusive; most large organisations will produce some blend of all three across different departments.
Consolidation

The most likely path, and the one consistent with a projected employment change of -1.6%. Assistants are not removed; they are spread thinner. One person covers three departments where they previously covered one, because the mechanical portion of each department's load has shrunk. Headcount declines slowly through attrition rather than redundancy — a post is not backfilled, a maternity cover is not extended, a retirement is absorbed. This is the quietest possible form of displacement and the hardest to detect in any dataset, because it never generates an announcement. It also degrades quietly: the coverage looks adequate until three departments have a crisis in the same week.
Professionalisation

The path Japan's AI Promotion Act appears to be legislating, in which coverage of the law's labour-market effects explicitly describes pushing remaining staff towards supervisory and judgement-based work. In this trajectory the role does not shrink; it is regraded. The four created tasks become the core of the job description rather than an unacknowledged overhead: knowledge-base owner, AI exception-handler, transcript custodian, first-line systems trainer. Titles change. Pay follows, eventually. This is the best outcome available to the occupation, and it is the one that requires an explicit institutional decision — it does not happen by default, because by default the extra work simply lands on the desk unremunerated.
Fragmentation

The path where the augmented eleven are unbundled and outsourced separately — scheduling to a service, inbox triage to a service, document management to a platform — leaving a residual on-site role built almost entirely from the traditional three: reception, forms, events. This trajectory preserves the fortress and destroys everything around it, producing a smaller, more physically anchored job with less career progression, because the tasks that led anywhere were the coordinating ones. It is the outcome most consistent with a purely cost-driven procurement process and least consistent with organisational memory, which is precisely the asset that fragmentation destroys and nobody prices.

The leading indicator to watch is not model capability, which will improve on a schedule nobody in this occupation controls. It is organisational integration. Gallup recorded 47% of workers saying their organisation had integrated AI tools to improve productivity, efficiency or quality, up six points from 41% in a single quarter — growth Gallup itself called sharp. If that rate of institutional adoption sustains, the resistance factor of 48% erodes not because anyone's mind changed about liability but because integrated tooling makes each subsequent deployment cheaper and each internal objection harder to sustain. If it plateaus, the current equilibrium holds for most of the decade.

The second indicator is contested and specific: whether reversals like Commonwealth Bank's become a pattern or remain an anomaly. One bank rescinding forty-five redundancy declarations within weeks, under union pressure and against its own operational data, is a data point. A dozen such reversals across two years would be a norm, and norms change board-level risk appetite far more effectively than any argument about the value of human judgement. The absence of union coverage across most of the American administrative workforce means the American version of that correction, if it comes, will have to arrive through operational failure rather than organised objection — which is slower, more expensive and considerably harder on the people involved.

The third indicator is the one this study can measure directly next year: whether the AI job creation index of 12% rises or falls. If it rises, augmentation is compounding — every new tool generates its own exception queue, its own verification burden, its own curation debt, and the role absorbs them. If it falls, the tools are maturing towards genuine autonomy and the human exception-handler is being designed out. Twelve per cent today, against 42% untouched and a resistance factor of 48%, describes an occupation being reshaped from the inside rather than removed from the outside.

None of this supports either of the two stories usually told about clerical work. It is not disappearing; a projected decline of 1.6% against a base of 1,944,000 is not a disappearance by any reasonable definition. Nor is it untouched; eleven of eighteen task clusters now begin with a machine draft, and the four newest tasks in the role exist only because machines make mistakes that matter. What is happening is narrower, slower and more consequential than either story: the work is being rebuilt around the parts a machine cannot do, and nobody has yet decided what those parts are worth.

sections.label: Challenge This Score
sections.title: The resistance factor is the number most likely to be wrong

blocks.text: An index of 30.2% is a claim, and claims should be contestable. This one rests on a decomposition of eighteen task clusters, an automation potential of 58% derived from evidence against ten vendors shipping in production, and a resistance factor of 48% assembled from liability, confidentiality, procurement and accountability constraints observed in deployment. Every one of those inputs is a judgement that a well-informed practitioner might make differently.

The judgements most exposed to challenge are three. First, the resistance factor: 48% is high, and it is the number that does the most work in pulling a 58% capability down to a 30.2% index. Anyone with direct evidence of organisations routing confidentiality-classified records or regulated form completion through automated systems at scale is holding data that would move it. Second, the treatment of the four created tasks: counting them at 12% assumes they persist rather than being absorbed by the next generation of tooling. Third, the traditional three: reception judgement, regulatory form completion and day-of event recovery are scored as untouched because no vendor evidence contradicts it, and absence of evidence in a fast-moving market is a weak claim.
If you do this work, or manage people who do, your operational experience is better evidence than any of it. Tell us where the model is wrong.
